'''''Pistacia chinensis''''', the '''Chinese pistache'''<ref>{{PLANTS|id=PICH4|taxon=Pistacia chinensis|accessdate=6 October 2015}}</ref> ({{zh|c=黄連木|p=huángliánmù}}), is a small to medium-sized tree in the [[genus]] ''[[Pistacia]]'' in the [[cashew]] family [[Anacardiaceae]], native to central and western [[China]].<ref name=eFloras>{{cite web|url=http://efloras.org/florataxon.aspx?flora_id=2&taxon_id=200012703 |title=''Pistacia chinensis'' Bunge, Enum. Pl. China Bor. 15. 1833 |author=Tianlu Min & Anders Barfod |work=Flora of China |publisher=Missouri Botanical Garden, St. Louis, MO & Harvard University Herbaria, Cambridge, MA |access-date=14 September 2012}}</ref> This species is planted as a street tree in temperate areas worldwide due to its attractive fruit and autumn foliage.

==Description==
[[File:Pistacia chinensis (Anacardiaceae) (tree).JPG|thumb|200px|Tree in the summer]]
It is [[Hardiness (plants)|hardy]], can withstand harsh conditions and poor quality soils, and grows up to {{convert|20|m|ft|abbr=on}}. The leaves are [[deciduous]], alternate, [[pinnate]], 20–25 cm long, with 10 or 12 leaflets, the terminal leaflet usually absent. The flowers are produced in [[panicle]]s {{convert|15-20|cm|in|abbr=on}} long at the ends of the branches; it is [[plant sexuality|dioecious]], with separate male and female plants.{{cn|date=June 2023}}

The fruit is a small red [[drupe]], turning blue when ripe, containing a single [[seed]].{{cn|date=June 2023}}

==Taxonomy==
Synonyms include: ''Pistacia formosana'' <small>Matsumura</small>; ''P. philippinensis'' <small>Merrill & Rolfe</small>; ''Rhus argyi'' <small>H. Léveillé</small>; ''R. gummifera'' <small>H. Léveillé</small>.<ref name=eFloras/>

Some botanists merge ''[[Pistacia integerrima]]'' into this species as the subspecies ''P. chinensis'' ssp. ''integerrima,'' with the plants considered here then becoming the subspecies ''P. chinensis'' ssp. ''chinensis.''{{cn|date=June 2023}}

==Distribution and habitat==
Its native range is on hill and mountain forests on rocky soils at {{convert|100-3600|m|ft|abbr=on}} above sea level. It is found in [[Mainland China]] (excluding the far north and the far west) and [[Taiwan]].<ref name=eFloras/>

==Invasiveness==

Chinese Pistache is an up-and-coming invasive species in the United States, especially in Texas. It invades natural areas negatively altering habitats for native animals and reduces biodiversity.<ref>{{cite web | title=Texas Invasives | url=https://www.texasinvasives.org/plant_database/detail.php?symbol=PICH4 }}</ref><ref>{{cite web | title=Chinese pistache: Pistacia chinensis (Sapindales: Anacardiaceae): Invasive Plant Atlas of the United States | url=https://www.invasiveplantatlas.org/subject.cfm?sub=14246 }}</ref>

==Ecology==
Chinese pistache grows best in full sun, being intolerant of shade; it is the most frost-tolerant species of ''[[Pistacia]]'', tolerating temperatures down to about -25 °C, yet it is most highly regarded in warm climates. It is planted for its impressive fall colors, which develop at least as far south as [[Orlando, Florida]].{{cn|date=June 2023}}

==Uses==
It is a popular choice for street trees in urban settings because it is very drought tolerant and can survive harsh environments. It is also used as an understock for ''[[Pistacia vera]]''.<ref>{{cite web | author=Ketzel Levine | title=Talking Plants: Pistacia_chinensis | url=https://www.npr.org/programs/talkingplants/profiles/pistaciachinensis.html | publisher=NPR| date=2003 | access-date=2009-11-11}}</ref> In China, the oil from the seeds is used for biodiesel production. The wood is used for production of furniture, and yields a yellow dye.<ref name=eFloras/>

It is also used in classical [[Chinese garden]] design.{{cn|date=June 2023}}
